theme: Judgment on the nations and Israel
readingInstruction: Read Amos 1:1-2:16. Amos, a shepherd from Judah, announces God’s judgment on the nations around Israel and then, to the shock of his hearers, on Israel itself. Notice the pattern: “For three transgressions… and for four.”
settingTheScene: Amos prophesied around 760 BC, during the reign of Jeroboam II, “two years before the earthquake.” He was not a professional prophet. He was a herdsman and dresser of sycamore figs from Tekoa in Judah, sent north to Israel. His message is one of the sharpest in the Bible: God demands justice, and ritual without righteousness is worthless. The book opens with a series of oracles on the surrounding nations, a pattern that draws Israel in.
observation: “The words of Amos, who was among the shepherds of Tekoa” (1:1).
“The LORD roars from Zion and utters his voice from Jerusalem” (1:2).
“For three transgressions of Damascus, and for four, I will not revoke the punishment” (1:3).
The same formula is repeated for Gaza, Tyre, Edom, Ammon, and Moab (1:6-2:3).
For Judah: “because they have rejected the law of the LORD, and have not kept his statutes” (2:4).
For Israel: “because they sell the righteous for silver, and the needy for a pair of sandals” (2:6).
“They trample the head of the poor into the dust of the earth and turn aside the way of the afflicted” (2:7).
“Also it was I who brought you up out of the land of Egypt” (2:10).
interpretation:
Amos begins like a preacher drawing a crowd. He starts with Israel’s enemies: Damascus, Gaza, Tyre, Edom, Ammon, Moab. His listeners would nod. These nations are guilty of brutality: threshing Gilead with iron sledges, selling whole communities as slaves, tearing open pregnant women, burning the bones of a king. God is a judge of the nations. They are accountable even though they do not have the law of Moses. There is a moral order that all people are expected to honor.

Then Amos turns to Judah, Israel’s southern cousin, and the crowd probably cheers. But the last oracle is the longest, and it is against Israel itself. The formula is the same. But the sins are different. The nations were accused of atrocities in war. Israel is accused of oppressing the poor in times of peace: selling the righteous for silver, trampling the needy, profaning God’s name through sexual exploitation, taking garments in pledge and drinking wine bought with fines. The sins are social and economic. They are everyday injustices committed under cover of respectable religion.

God reminds them of his grace: “It was I who brought you up out of the land of Egypt.” He destroyed the Amorites before them. He raised up prophets and Nazirites. They have responded by making the Nazirites drink wine and silencing the prophets. This is the heart of the charge. Privilege increases responsibility. “You only have I known of all the families of the earth” (3:2). Having received more, they are held to a higher standard.

The consequence is a judgment so complete that “the one who is stout of heart among the mighty shall flee away naked.” No strength will help.

The message of Amos is that God cares about how we treat each other. A faith that has no effect on how we treat the poor is not faith. The same God who roars from Zion is the God who sees the needy sold for a pair of sandals.
connection: James 1:27 says that pure religion is to visit orphans and widows in their affliction. Jesus said, “Everyone to whom much was given, of him much will be required” (Luke 12:48). Amos speaks to the problem Jesus addressed in Matthew 23:23: neglecting justice, mercy, and faithfulness while tithing mint and dill. 1 Peter 4:17 says that judgment begins at the household of God. Jesus came to proclaim good news to the poor (Luke 4:18).
application:
Ask whether your faith has any effect on how you treat the poor and the vulnerable.

Examine your business or workplace dealings. Is there any unfairness you tolerate?

Remember that you have been given much. What does that require?
prayerPrompts: Ask him to let your faith show in how you treat the vulnerable.
Thank him for bringing his people home.
